neurological_exam.gait: Reduced stride length bilaterally with marked reduction of left arm swing; right arm swing mildly reduced. Stooped posture. Pull test: two retropulsive steps before recovery. Falls history: two falls in the past three months, both occurring during gait freezing episodes at narrow spaces.
neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (fails to habituate after 10 taps). Seborrheic dermatitis on scalp and nasolabial folds. Micrographia demonstrated on writing sample — letters progressively smaller and trailing off. No myoclonus. End-of-dose symptom diary reviewed: patient documents return of stiffness, tremor, and freezing approximately 2.5 hours after each levodopa dose, lasting 30-45 minutes prior to next dose ('OFF' periods 4 times daily).

patient.chief_complaint: Worsening motor fluctuations with predictable OFF periods and freezing of gait despite current levodopa regimen
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Rosa Elena Vega is a 58-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with a 4-year history of Parkinson's disease who presents to the movement disorders clinic accompanied by her husband for evaluation of worsening motor fluctuations and increasingly frequent freezing of gait. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 54 following a 12- to 18-month history of progressive left hand rest tremor, left arm stiffness, and generalized slowing. At diagnosis she had an excellent response to levodopa with greater than 50% improvement in motor scores and was titrated to her current regimen of carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg four times daily. For approximately the first two years she had excellent motor control throughout the day. However, over the past 18 months she has noticed that the benefit from each levodopa dose seems to wear off approximately 2.5 hours after ingestion. She keeps a symptom diary and consistently notes return of left-hand tremor, bilateral stiffness, bradykinesia, and freezing episodes during these predictable OFF windows. The OFF periods last approximately 30 to 45 minutes until the next dose takes effect. She reports four distinct OFF periods per day, each associated with subjective stiffness, slowing, difficulty initiating movement, and two to three freezing-of-gait episodes per week. She has had two actual falls in the past three months, occurring when she froze while walking through doorways. She denies any involuntary writhing movements (dyskinesias) at peak dose. Her husband reports that during OFF periods she is visibly more rigid and speaks more softly, and that her facial expression becomes even more mask-like. She denies any visual hallucinations, significant cognitive complaints beyond occasional word-finding difficulty, or urinary incontinence. She reports long-standing constipation predating her PD diagnosis by approximately five years, managed with fiber supplementation. She also notes hyposmia for at least six to seven years, which she initially attributed to chronic allergies. She has a history of chronic migraine and uses sumatriptan for acute attacks. Approximately twice per month she requires prochlorperazine 10 mg for severe nausea accompanying migraines, a practice that predates her PD diagnosis by several years. Her husband and her neurologist are concerned that the prochlorperazine use could be contributing to worsening Parkinsonian symptoms. Her hypothyroidism was diagnosed three years ago and she is currently taking levothyroxine 75 mcg daily; her most recent TSH was measured six months ago. She denies new medications, recent infections, or other intercurrent illnesses. A maternal history of Parkinson's disease has made her particularly anxious about disease progression.

output.proposed: Carbidopa-levodopa (current) with evaluation of prochlorperazine (current as-needed medication) and sumatriptan (current as-needed medication)
interactions: Prochlorperazine is a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (phenothiazine antipsychotic class); concurrent use with levodopa produces pharmacological antagonism at the dopamine receptor level
Sumatriptan (5-HT1B/1D agonist) has no significant pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction with levodopa or carbidopa
Levothyroxine absorption may be reduced by concurrent calcium or iron supplements; take separately from carbidopa-levodopa by at least 30 minutes to avoid potential interference
contraindications: Prochlorperazine is contraindicated in patients with Parkinson's disease due to its central dopamine D2 receptor blocking mechanism, which directly antagonizes levodopa's therapeutic effect
All phenothiazines and most butyrophenones are contraindicated in PD for the same mechanism
warnings: Even intermittent use of prochlorperazine (twice monthly) can worsen motor control in PD patients and complicate assessment of levodopa adequacy
Prochlorperazine can cause acute dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia in addition to worsening parkinsonism
Drug-induced worsening of PD symptoms may persist for days to weeks after a prochlorperazine dose in sensitive patients
output.formulary_status: Prochlorperazine — available but contraindicated in PD
alternatives: Ondansetron 4-8 mg orally as needed for nausea (5-HT3 antagonist; no dopaminergic effect; preferred in PD)
Domperidone (peripheral D2 antagonist; does not cross blood-brain barrier — not FDA-approved in the US but available internationally)
Metoclopramide is similarly contraindicated in PD (also a dopamine antagonist)
Trimethobenzamide 300 mg orally for mild nausea — no dopaminergic effect

results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease
results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M, et al.
results.key_finding: Clinically established PD requires bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, with at least two supportive criteria (clear levodopa response, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, rest tremor of a limb, olfactory loss) and no absolute exclusion criteria. Clear levodopa response is a major supportive criterion.

results.title: Challenges in the Diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease
results.authors: Tolosa E, Wenning G, Poewe W
results.key_finding: Wearing-off (end-of-dose deterioration) occurs in up to 50% of PD patients within 5 years of initiating levodopa therapy. Management strategies include fractionating levodopa doses, adding catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors (entacapone), adding MAO-B inhibitors, or introducing dopamine agonists. Predictable wearing-off differs from random motor fluctuations.

results.title: Parkinson's Disease is Overdiagnosed Clinically at Baseline in Diagnostically Uncertain Cases
results.authors: Marshall VL, Patterson J, Hadley DM, et al.
results.key_finding: DaTscan (I-123 ioflupane SPECT) identifies presynaptic dopaminergic deficit with high sensitivity and specificity for neurodegenerative parkinsonism. Drug-induced parkinsonism (including from phenothiazines and metoclopramide) shows a normal DaTscan in the absence of underlying neurodegenerative disease.

sequence_constraints.reason: Baseline labs including TSH should be reviewed alongside drug interaction check to fully characterize modifiable contributors to motor worsening before therapy adjustment
Exclude vascular parkinsonism, structural mimics, and atypical features on MRI before committing to DaTscan interpretation within a PD framework

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: confirm clinically established PD with bradykinesia plus resting tremor and rigidity, prior clear levodopa response (supportive criterion), and absence of absolute exclusion criteria

Recognize prochlorperazine as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (phenothiazine class) that is contraindicated in PD and can worsen motor symptoms even with intermittent use; substitute ondansetron for migraine-associated nausea

Identify elevated TSH (5.8 mIU/L) indicating suboptimal levothyroxine replacement; adjust levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 6 weeks, as hypothyroidism can independently worsen fatigue and motor slowing
Characterize motor fluctuations as predictable end-of-dose wearing-off based on symptom diary and initiate appropriate management (fractionated dosing, COMT inhibitor, or MAO-B inhibitor)
Verify correct timing of levothyroxine (empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before carbidopa-levodopa) to prevent absorption interference
Document pre-motor features (anosmia, constipation) predating PD diagnosis by 5-7 years as supportive of idiopathic synucleinopathy rather than drug-induced parkinsonism
Assess fall risk formally and refer to physical therapy for gait and balance training including freezing-of-gait strategies
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, promethazine, or other phenothiazine/butyrophenone antiemetics in a patient with Parkinson's disease

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — restrict psychosis pharmacotherapy to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient with PD-MCI or cognitive impairment

Do not attribute the totality of motor worsening to drug-induced parkinsonism from prochlorperazine without DaTscan confirmation — the temporal profile, asymmetry, and pre-motor history indicate established underlying PD
key_reasoning_points: Predictable end-of-dose wearing-off emerging 4 years after PD diagnosis is a classic pharmacokinetic complication of levodopa therapy, not a sign of misdiagnosis

Prochlorperazine (a phenothiazine dopamine D2 antagonist) used intermittently for migraine nausea is contraindicated in PD and can significantly worsen motor symptoms; it is the primary actionable drug red herring

DaTscan asymmetry — right posterior putamen more affected — is contralateral to the clinically dominant left-sided signs, consistent with idiopathic PD lateralization and not drug-induced parkinsonism (which yields a normal DaTscan)

Elevated TSH (5.8 mIU/L) is an important actionable finding; suboptimal thyroid replacement is an independent reversible contributor to fatigue and motor slowing but does not explain the tremor, asymmetry, or levodopa responsiveness
Pre-motor features (anosmia for 6-7 years, constipation for 5 years) predating PD diagnosis and prochlorperazine use support underlying synucleinopathy not drug-induced parkinsonism

Loss of bilateral swallow-tail sign on SWI provides imaging-level supportive evidence for nigrosomal degeneration consistent with PD, distinguishing it from essential tremor (which would show a normal swallow-tail)
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Parkinson's disease is a clinical diagnosis under the MDS criteria; laboratory testing excludes a mimic when one is suspected.

red_herrings.data_point: Active intermittent prochlorperazine use (10 mg up to twice monthly) for migraine nausea
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest that motor worsening is drug-induced parkinsonism from prochlorperazine rather than true PD progression, leading to delay in optimizing levodopa therapy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prochlorperazine is a genuine concern and should be discontinued and replaced; however, the documented pre-motor features preceding drug use, the asymmetric onset, the clear prior levodopa response, and the abnormal DaTscan with contralateral right-predominant deficit all confirm established idiopathic PD rather than pure drug-induced parkinsonism

red_herrings.data_point: Elevated TSH at 5.8 mIU/L on levothyroxine therapy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all motor slowing, fatigue, and worsening to undertreated hypothyroidism and defer levodopa optimization
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Suboptimal thyroid replacement warrants levothyroxine dose adjustment but cannot account for the unilateral rest tremor, asymmetric bradykinesia, freezing of gait, or levodopa responsiveness; hypothyroidism is a co-contributor to non-specific fatigue only

red_herrings.data_point: Maternal family history of Parkinson's disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raise concern for genetic/familial PD requiring special workup (e.g., LRRK2, GBA genetic testing) that would delay standard management
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A positive family history of PD increases prior probability of idiopathic PD but does not change the standard diagnostic workup or alter the primary diagnosis of idiopathic PD; genetic testing is not required for clinical diagnosis per MDS 2015 criteria
